etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English bounsen, bunsen (“to beat, thump”), cognate with Scots bunce, bonce (“to bounce”). Of uncertain origin. Perhaps imitative, related to bump, or related to Middle English bonchen (“to pound, beat”) and Dutch bonken (“to bump”).

Compare Saterland Frisian bumzje (“to pound, bang, bounce”), West Frisian bûnzje (“to throb, bounce, pulsate”), Dutch bonzen (“to thump, knock, throb, bounce”), German Low German bunsen, bumsen (“to beat, bounce”), German bumsen (“to thud, bang, pound”).

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To change the direction of motion after hitting an obstacle.
(intransitive) To move quickly up and then down (or vice versa), once or repeatedly.

quote.citation: 2012 May 13, Alistair Magowan, “Sunderland 0-1 Man Utd”, in BBC Sport‎[1]:
quote.text: The Black Cats contributed to their own downfall for the only goal when Titus Bramble, making his first appearance since Boxing Day, and Michael Turner, let Phil Jones' cross bounce across the six-yard box as Rooney tucked in at the back post.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause to move quickly up and down, or back and forth, once or repeatedly.
(transitive, colloquial) To suggest or introduce (an idea, etc.) to (off or by) someone, in order to gain feedback.
(intransitive) To leap or spring suddenly or unceremoniously; to bound.

quote.citation: 1731, On Mr. Pulteney's Being Put Out of the Council, Jonathan Swift:

definitions.definition: To move rapidly (between).

quote.citation: 2017 July 30, Ali Barthwell, “Ice and fire finally meet in a front-loaded episode of Game Of Thrones (newbies)”, in The Onion AV Club‎[2]:
quote.text: “The Queen’s Justice” had some fantastic moments of wit and heart but the structure and pacing didn’t do it any favors. The first section of the episode mostly bounced between Jon Snow’s arrival at Dragonstone and Cersei Lannister burning through her enemies and giving nary a fuck.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, informal, of a cheque/check) To be refused by a bank because it is drawn on insufficient funds.
(transitive, informal) To fail to cover (have sufficient funds for) (a draft presented against one's account).
(intransitive, slang) To leave.

quote.citation: 2006, Noire [pseudonym], Thug-A-Licious: An Urban Erotic Tale, New York, N.Y.: One World, Ballantine Books, →ISBN, page 64:
quote.text: I was definitely looking forward to getting me some more of Yasmere in the future, so I took a quick second to give her a last little bit of love before I bounced.

quote.citation: 2023, Nathan Bryon, Tom Melia, directed by Raine Allen-Miller, Rye Lane, spoken by Nathan (Simon Manyonda):
quote.text: All right, look, don't prang out. They had this paint-party-brunch thing. But I only stayed for 45 minutes, painted a tiny bit of a door, ate half an almond croissant and bounced.

definitions.definition: (US, slang, dated) To eject violently, as from a room; to discharge unceremoniously, as from employment.

quote.text: Nobody took umbrage and bounced me out of the Union for being a pro.

quote.citation: 1977 December 17, Tom Hurley, “The Evolution of Sporters”, in Gay Community News, volume 5, number 24, page 12:
quote.text: Anyone who gets bounced out of [this bar] is not just pushed onto the street — he is walked home, or put in a cab.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, slang, African-American Vernacular, sometimes followed by with) To have sexual intercourse.
(transitive, air combat) To attack unexpectedly.
(intransitive, electronics) To turn power off and back on; to reset.
(transitive, intransitive, Internet, of an e-mail message) To return undelivered.
(intransitive, aviation) To land hard and lift off again due to excess momentum.
(intransitive, skydiving) To land hard at unsurvivable velocity with fatal results.
(transitive, sound recording) To mix (two or more tracks of a multi-track audio tape recording) and record the result onto a single track, in order to free up tracks for further material to be added.
(slang, archaic) To bully; to scold.

quote.citation: 1621 (first performance), John Fletcher, “The Wild-Goose Chase; a Comedy”, in Comedies and Tragedies […], London:  […]  Humphrey Robinson, […], and for Humphrey Moseley […], published 1679, →OCLC, (please specify the act number in uppercase Roman numerals, and the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: Would I had him here again, I would so bounce him , I would so thank his lordship for his lewd plot.

definitions.definition: (slang, archaic) To boast; to bluster.
(archaic) To strike or thump, so as to rebound, or to make a sudden noise; to knock loudly.

quote.text: Another bounces as hard as he can knock.

definitions.definition: (horse racing, slang) To race poorly after a successful race.
(music, technology) To render multiple tracks to computer storage so that they can be played back and re-recorded with the addition of further material.
A change of direction of motion after hitting the ground or an obstacle.

quote.citation: 2012 June 9, Owen Phillips, “Euro 2012: Netherlands 0-1 Denmark”, in BBC Sport:
quote.text: Krohn-Dehli took advantage of a lucky bounce of the ball after a battling run on the left flank by Simon Poulsen, dummied two defenders and shot low through goalkeeper Maarten Stekelenburg's legs after 24 minutes.

definitions.definition: A movement up and then down (or vice versa), once or repeatedly.
(Internet) An email that returns to the sender because of a delivery failure.

(quantum mechanics) A hypothetical event where a collapsing system, such as a universe in the Big Bounce theory, reaches a point of extreme density and then rebounds back into an expanding phase, essentially reversing the contraction due to quantum mechanical effects.
(slang) The sack, dismissal.

quote.citation: 2007, Annabelle Gurwitch, Fired!: Tales of the Canned, Canceled, Downsized, and Dismissed, page 243:
quote.text: Someone more clever than I said, "It's not the bounce that counts, it's the bounce back. "
Customers said I was a hoot; management gave me the bounce.

quote.citation: 2018, Harry Stephen Keeler, The Portrait of Jirjohn Cobb, page 241:
quote.text: I was no longer with the Oakhaven Hospital when I decided to come out here to the island; they'd fired me when they traced a long-distance call I'd made to San Francisco, under the director's name, to a man the papers had said got pinched out there, under suspicion of having lifted a poke with 10 grand in it—but later released—a man named Andy Glover. I thought sure he was a certain lug who'd been in stir with me, and thought to make a touch—however, skip it!—the point is that it was the wrong Andy Glover!—the call got traced to the phone in the hospital urinal room—and I got the bounce.

definitions.definition: (archaic) A bang, boom.

quote.citation: 1773, Oliver Goldsmith, She Stoops to Conquer:
quote.text: I don't value her resentment the bounce of a cracker.

definitions.definition: (archaic) A drink based on brandy.W

quote.citation: 1870 May, “Irish Life”, in The Saint Pauls Magazine, volume VI, London: Strahan & Co., publishers, 56, Ludgate Hill, →OCLC, page 203:
quote.text: A prologue of cherry bounce,—brandy,—preceded the entertainment, which was enlivened by hob-nobs and joyous toasts.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter VI, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: He had one hand on the bounce bottle—and he'd never let go of that since he got back to the table—but he had a handkerchief in the other and was swabbing his deadlights with it.

definitions.definition: (archaic) A heavy, sudden, and often noisy, blow or thump.

quote.text: The bounce burst ope the door.

definitions.definition: (archaic) Bluster; brag; untruthful boasting; audacious exaggeration; an impudent lie; a bouncer.

quote.citation: 1827, Thomas De Quincey, On Murder Considered as one of the Fine Arts:
quote.text: And, in fact, the whole story is a bounce of his own. For, in a most abusive letter which he wrote “to a learned person,” (meaning Wallis the mathematician,) he gives quite another account of the matter
